task_description: Pulmonary toxicity prediction — predict whether a drug causes toxic damage to the lungs or respiratory system (e.g., interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, pneumonitis, respiratory depression, bronchospasm)
prediction_question: Does this molecule exhibit pulmonary toxicity? Your final answer should be formatted as either: 'Final answer: Toxicity' or 'Final answer: Non-toxicity'.

EGFR.role: Receptor tyrosine kinase; alveolar epithelial repair
EGFR.logic: EGFR signaling drives proliferation and repair of alveolar type II pneumocytes after epithelial injury. Strong binding at the EGFR ATP site inhibits this regenerative response, and impaired alveolar epithelial repair underlies interstitial lung disease and pneumonitis. Weak binding leaves the repair pathway intact.
EGFR.role_cited: Receptor tyrosine kinase[3t]; alveolar epithelial repair[4t]
EGFR.logic_cited: EGFR signaling drives proliferation and repair of alveolar type II pneumocytes after epithelial injury[4]. Strong binding at the EGFR ATP site inhibits this regenerative response[3], and impaired alveolar epithelial repair underlies interstitial lung disease and pneumonitis. VEGFR2.role: Endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase; pulmonary vascular integrity
VEGFR2.logic: VEGFR2 (KDR) mediates endothelial survival signaling that maintains the alveolar-capillary barrier. Strong binding at the VEGFR2 ATP site blocks this survival signal and destabilizes the endothelium, contributing to pulmonary hypertension, pleural effusion and pulmonary edema. Weak binding leaves barrier maintenance intact.
VEGFR2.role_cited: Endothelial receptor tyrosine kinase[5c]; pulmonary vascular integrity[5c]
VEGFR2.logic_cited: VEGFR2 (KDR) mediates endothelial survival signaling that maintains the alveolar-capillary barrier[5c]. Strong binding at the VEGFR2 ATP site blocks this survival signal[5c] and destabilizes the endothelium[5c], contributing to pulmonary hypertension, pleural effusion[6t] and pulmonary edema[6t]. Weak binding leaves barrier maintenance intact.

ACE.role: Peptidase (kininase II); degrades bradykinin and substance P in lung
ACE.logic: ACE degrades bradykinin and substance P in the pulmonary vasculature and airways. Strong binding at the catalytic zinc site blocks this degradation, so the peptides accumulate, sensitize airway sensory nerves and cause persistent dry cough and occasional angioedema. Weak binding does not perturb pulmonary kinin turnover.

ACE.logic_cited: ACE degrades bradykinin and substance P in the pulmonary vasculature and airways[8t]. mTOR.role: Serine/threonine kinase; cell growth and immune regulation
mTOR.logic: mTOR regulates growth, proliferation and autophagy in alveolar epithelial and immune cells. Strong binding at the mTOR kinase site suppresses these programs and is associated with lymphocytic alveolitis and non-infectious interstitial pneumonitis. Weak binding leaves alveolar immune homeostasis intact.

mTOR.logic_cited: mTOR regulates growth, proliferation and autophagy in alveolar epithelial and immune cells[11t]. Strong binding at the mTOR kinase site suppresses these programs[12] and is associated with lymphocytic alveolitis and non-infectious interstitial pneumonitis[13]. Weak binding leaves alveolar immune homeostasis intact.

pathway_rules: Blocking alveolar epithelial repair (EGFR) or endothelial survival signaling (VEGFR2) prevents regeneration of the alveolar-capillary unit, the mechanism of drug-induced interstitial lung disease, pneumonitis and pulmonary edema.
Blocking pulmonary ACE lets bradykinin and substance P accumulate in the airway wall, sensitizing sensory C-fibers and causing persistent dry cough and angioedema.
Suppressing mTOR-dependent growth and autophagy in alveolar epithelium and lung immune cells promotes lymphocytic alveolitis and non-infectious pneumonitis.

Injury is also produced outside these four targets: depression of brainstem respiratory drive, reactive-metabolite or oxidant damage to alveolar epithelium, lysosomal phospholipid accumulation in alveolar macrophages, and embolic obstruction of pulmonary capillaries by oily depot vehicles.

The lung defends itself continuously: alveolar macrophages phagocytose and degrade material reaching the alveolar surface, the mucociliary escalator clears the airways, and the pulmonary endothelium metabolizes and inactivates circulating xenobiotics on first pass. This reserve absorbs ordinary drug exposure, so parenchymal or airway injury appears only when one of the mechanisms above is actively engaged; a molecule that engages none of them leaves lung structure and function unchanged.

yes_features: Fused 1,4-benzodiazepine ring, with or without a triazolo or imidazo ring fused to it: depresses the brainstem respiratory rhythm and causes dose-dependent hypoventilation.
Opioid agonist scaffold — morphinan, 4-aryl- or 4-anilido-piperidine, or diphenylheptanone: suppresses the medullary response to CO2, causing respiratory depression and arrest.
Bis(2-chloroethyl)amine or oxazaphosphorine ring: alkylates alveolar epithelium and capillary endothelium, giving pneumonitis that can progress to pulmonary fibrosis.
Antifolate — a 2,4-diaminopteridine or fused pyrimidine linked to a benzoyl-glutamate arm: causes hypersensitivity pneumonitis and interstitial lung disease independent of cumulative dose.
Purine bearing a sulfur substituent at the 6-position: thiopurine immunosuppression is associated with reversible interstitial pneumonitis.

ATP-competitive kinase inhibitor head — a 2-aminopyrimidine or 2-anilinopyrimidine fused to a bicyclic heteroaryl, an N-alkoxy benzamide MEK head, or an acrylamide covalent warhead on an amino-heterocycle: interstitial lung disease is a recognized class effect of CDK4/6, MEK, BTK and multi-kinase inhibitors.

Straight-chain aliphatic acyl ester of eight carbons or longer on a steroid or neuroleptic alcohol: this oily intramuscular depot design can enter the venous circulation and lodge in pulmonary capillaries as microemboli, causing cough, dyspnea and syncope after injection.

Tricyclic fused aromatic system (phenothiazine, thieno-benzodiazepine, dibenz-oxazepine or -azepine) carrying a protonatable amine on a short side chain: this cationic amphiphile is trapped in lysosomes of alveolar macrophages and type II pneumocytes and produces phospholipidosis and alveolitis.
no_features: Four-membered beta-lactam fused to a thiazolidine or dihydrothiazine ring and bearing a free carboxylate (penicillin or cephalosporin): acts on bacterial transpeptidase, stays ionized and is renally cleared within hours.

Nitro group attached to an imidazole or other azole ring of an antimicrobial scaffold: reduction to a reactive species requires the low-redox-potential ferredoxin systems of anaerobic organisms and does not occur in oxygenated lung tissue.

Endogenous metabolite or close analogue — amino acid, nucleobase, simple sugar or polyol, vitamin, or seco-steroid: distribution and elimination follow physiological transporter and renal routes without lung retention.

Azole ring joined to a tertiary carbinol or a benzylic nitrile in an antifungal or aromatase-inhibitor scaffold: the target is a fungal or steroidogenic cytochrome P450 that has no counterpart in alveolar epithelium or endothelium.

Multiply ionized polar structure — geminal bisphosphonate, biphenyl-tetrazole, quaternary ammonium, or a zwitterion with two or more acid groups: low passive permeability confines the compound near extracellular water and prevents accumulation in lung lipid.

Steroid nucleus carrying only small polar groups (11-hydroxy or 11-keto, 16,17-acetonide, free hydroxyl, or a short C2-C4 ester): these receptor agonists suppress alveolar inflammatory transcription and are the standard treatment for inflammatory and fibrosing lung disease.

Small single-ring anilide, phenol, oxazolone or simple azine/azole scaffold cleared by direct glucuronidation or sulfation: conjugative elimination competes with oxidative bioactivation, so no reactive intermediate reaches alveolar tissue.

Simple inorganic salt or a small radiolabelled tracer analogue given at sub-pharmacological diagnostic doses: the administered amount is orders of magnitude below any dose that could injure lung tissue.
